bullets.t: This small three-roomed shrine was built by Sety II, about 1200 to 1194 BC, as a resting place for the portable boats of Amun, Mut and Khonsu on festival days.
The gods travelled in boat-shaped shrines called barks, carried on priests' shoulders. Digital Karnak gives the west room to Mut, the middle to Amun and the east to Khonsu.
The site board calls these the Chapels of Sety I. Scholars, including Chevrier who published the shrine in 1940, give it to Sety II. Sety I built the Hypostyle Hall ahead.
It stands almost complete, which is rare here. The foundations, door sills and first course are hard quartzite, the rest sandstone. One corner and the west wall were left undressed.
When built it stood outside the temple's west entrance, in front of the Second Pylon. About 250 years later Shoshenq I built the great court around it, so it now sits inside.
Digital Karnak suggests ordinary Egyptians, kept out of the inner temple, may have gathered here to pray, close to where the gods paused on their journeys.
Look for Sety II himself in the reliefs on the south face and by the entrance, offering to the Theban gods.
When Nectanebo I built the First Pylon, about 380 BC, this shrine may have been partly taken down for the work, and was then only partly rebuilt.

kids.t: Count the doorways of the little shrine: one for each god's boat. How many can you find?

sety2.look: The low, flat-topped stone building with three doorways side by side on the left (north) side of the court. Stand in the middle of the court to see all three together.
sety2.note: In the open court beside the main route. The doorways may be roped off; if so, see it from the court, where all three doors face you.

bullets.t: This lone column is all that stands of Taharqa's kiosk, built between 690 and 664 BC: two rows of five papyrus columns, each about 21 metres tall.
Taharqa was a Kushite pharaoh from Nubia, in modern Sudan, of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty. He ruled both lands, and he also built a pyramid at Nuri in Sudan.
Each column is almost 3 metres across. The gap between the two rows is over 16 metres, too wide for stone roof beams, so scholars think the kiosk was never roofed.
Stand at the base and look up. Twenty-one metres is roughly a seven-storey building, and the flower-shaped top is an open papyrus bloom.
Nobody is sure what it was for. A calcite shrine at the centre once held the god's bark, and some scholars link it to a yearly 'union of the disc' rite for Amun-Ra's statue.
Excavation suggests a wooden kiosk stood on this spot first, and the calcite altar probably belonged to it. Taharqa's stone kiosk replaced it.
More than four centuries later, Ptolemy IV added carvings of nome-gods, the gods of Egypt's regions, to the low screen walls. The pink granite paving may date from then too.
Taharqa is in the Bible as 'Tirhakah king of Ethiopia' (2 Kings 19:9), who marched against Assyria in 701 BC. But he became king only about 690 BC, so scholars debate how that fits.

kids.t: Find the one very tall column standing all alone in the middle, with a flower on top. Wave to it!

kids: Find the low stumps on the ground where the other nine columns once stood. Can you hop from one to the next?
taharqa.look: The single tall column with a flower-shaped top, alone in the middle of the court. Low stumps and a pale calcite altar around it mark the other nine columns.
taharqa.note: In the open court, on the main route. Nothing to enter, so access is not a concern; the column is visible from anywhere in the court.

bullets.t: Ramesses III, who reigned about 1184 to 1153 BC, built this complete small temple as a bark shrine: a way station for the gods' boats on festival days.
It follows the classic temple plan in miniature: a small pylon, an open court, a little pillared hall, then three sanctuaries, all within about 60 metres.
The little pylon is carved with the king smiting his enemies. It had a granite gateway but no flagstaffs. Two standing statues of the king flank the doorway.

Inside the court, statues of the king stand against the pillars in the form of Osiris, god of death and rebirth. Digital Karnak counts sixteen; other descriptions give fewer, so count them yourselves.
At the back, the holy of holies was replaced by three bark shrines, for Amun, Mut and Khonsu: the same three gods as in Sety II's shrine opposite.
The temple sits at right angles to the main east-west route. It is also set opposite Sety II's shrine, so the barks of the same three gods could pause on either side.
The pillared hall is 21 metres wide but only 9 deep. Digital Karnak shows squat columns here, a good contrast with the giant ones in the Hypostyle Hall ahead.
About 240 years later, Shoshenq I built his great court around the front half of this temple, so the pylon end is inside the court and the rest reaches out to the south.
Ramesses III also began the Temple of Khonsu in the south of the precinct, a larger and better preserved temple of the same king that the family can see later.

kids.t: Count the tall statues of the king standing in rows in the court, with arms crossed on their chests.
Find the two big standing statues beside the doorway of the little pylon.

ram3.look: The little temple entered from the right (south) side of the court: two statues beside a small pylon doorway, then a court lined with the king's statues.
ram3.note: Partly shaded inside. The inner rooms may be gated or roped off; if so, look in from the pylon doorway, where the statue-lined court and the sanctuary doors are in view.

bullets.t: On the outer wall by this doorway Shoshenq I recorded his campaign into Canaan, about 925 BC: the king smiting enemies above rings naming about 156 captured towns.
Each oval ring is shaped like a fort wall and holds a place name, topped by a bound captive. Amun and the goddess of Thebes hold the cords that tie them.

Shoshenq is usually identified with Shishak, who took treasures from Jerusalem in 1 Kings 14:25 to 26. Jerusalem is not on the surviving list, and scholars debate why, and how reliable the Bible's account is.
The relief is carved on the south face of the court wall, outside the doorway, not inside the court. Look to either side of the door as you go through.
The portal fills the gap between the Second Pylon and Ramesses III's temple. It is just under 5 metres wide and was designed as part of the court wall, marked inside by two papyrus columns.
A quarry stela from Gebel el-Silsila, dated to his year 21, records a new sandstone quarry for a pylon and festival hall at Karnak, for his 'first campaign of victory'.
A fragment of a victory stela with Shoshenq's name was found at Megiddo in 1925. Some scholars now suggest it may be part of a building instead.
It is called Bubastite after Bubastis, the Nile Delta city that was the home of Shoshenq's family, who were of Libyan descent.

kids.t: Find the biggest figure on the wall: a king raising his arm over tiny enemies. Can you copy his pose?
Look for the little ovals packed in rows. Each one has a town name inside.

bubastite.look: The doorway in the south-east corner of the court, with a tall column inside it. Go through and turn to the wall beside the door: the king strides over rows of name rings.
bubastite.note: The doorway leads out of the court, and the relief is on its outer face. It may be closed or roped off; if so, see the doorway from inside the court.
